turn_text: So this sort of compromise that is I guess come up late last month came from House leadership, the so-called kitchen sink package. What are the problems there and what are the hurdles? I mean, I mentioned in the intro that it's probably not going to get a
it might be done in arrival. But can you sort of tease that out and what more than anything, what the real problem is there?

Absolutely. So first, and I would say that House leadership, the Speaker, the Chair of the House Administration Committee have put this forth as this notion of a compromise package, but it isn't. There's no compromise between any parties because people who've been working on this issue and prioritizing this issue were not included in House leadership's effort to direct this. Among the things that occurred is for starters, those who have been really digging into this issue legislatively were cut out of the process. It was a leadership-driven effort, which at times can be uh, you know, it should be viewed with times of a wary eye. And in this case, it was the case. So we know that, you know, many Republicans, again, my bill as an example is wholly bipartisan. There are other bipartisan bills that address the similar issue. But yet when this process was moved forward, it included not just the House of Representatives, but also the executive branch and the judicial branch. Now, independent of anything, I do think that we need major reforms within the judiciary. But two problems. One, we know that many Republicans have a very bright line at wanting to address issues within Congress, so banning members of Congress from selling stocks and not address other branches at this time. So we knew that was a poison pill for many of the Republicans who otherwise support the bill and are co-sponsors of stock banning bills or stock trade bills. Notably, the provisions related to the executive branch actually would decrease the level of ethics requirements that exist within the executive branch where there's already really pretty strong ethics requirements. And by putting them at this new level that was being put forth by a house administration, we'd actually be degrading the level of ethics requirements for executive branch. And then notably, one of the provisions allows for the creation of line trust, but as they are defined in this legislation they're not qualified blind trust they are basically blind trusts. That can be called blind trust, essentially, if, if the majority vote within Congress, or the Office of Ethics, and the executive branch just decides it is. So there's, you know, an actual standard for what constitutes a blind trust. In this case, we would be doing this legislation would be degrading that. that trust and essentially whatever is blessed by the majority vote within Congress could all of a sudden be called a blind trust. That means you could have a child run it, you could have a family member, you could maintain contact with whoever is running your quote unquote blind trust and really degrading what is generally understood and legally recognized as a blind trust.
